Pale
payl
a. (wan; deficient in colour)
Latin pallidus, pale, wan. The Authorized Version uses the adjective twice, and they are the two poles of the word: a promise that Jacob's face shall not wax pale, and the colour of the horse whose rider is Death.

Biblical Definition

Paleness in Scripture is the colour of fear and of shame drained into the face. Isaiah announces the end of it for the covenant people: “Therefore thus saith the LORD, who redeemed Abraham, concerning the house of Jacob, Jacob shall not now be ashamed, neither shall his face now wax pale” (Isaiah 29:22). The ground of the promise is redemption already accomplished — who redeemed Abraham — and the effect is on the countenance, because shame is a thing that shows. Over against it stands the fourth seal: “And I looked, and behold a pale horse: and his name that sat on him was Death, and Hell followed with him” (Revelation 6:8). The Greek is chloros, the greenish pallor of a corpse; John gives the rider a name, which none of the other three receive, and a power limited to the fourth part of the earth. Between these two verses the believer lives: Death rides pale, and the redeemed face does not.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines pale as white or whitish; wan; deficient in color; not ruddy or fresh of color.

expand to see more

PALE, a. White or whitish; wan; deficient in color; not ruddy or fresh of color; as, a pale face.

PALE, a. Not bright; not shining; of a faint lustre; dim; as, the pale light of the moon.

WAN, a. Pale; having a sickly hue; languid of look.

WAX, v.i. To increase in size; to grow; to become; as, to wax pale; to wax old.

ASHAMED, a. Affected by shame; abashed or confused by guilt or a conviction of some criminal action.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 29:22 — "Therefore thus saith the LORD, who redeemed Abraham, concerning the house of Jacob, Jacob shall not now be ashamed, neither shall his face now wax pale."

Revelation 6:8 — "And I looked, and behold a pale horse: and his name that sat on him was Death, and Hell followed with him. And power was given unto them over the fourth part of the earth, to kill with sword, and with hunger, and with death, and with the beasts of the earth."

Isaiah 29:23 — "But when he seeth his children, the work of mine hands, in the midst of him, they shall sanctify my name, and sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and shall fear the God of Israel."

Revelation 6:7 — "And when he had opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth beast say, Come and see."

Modern Corruption

Death is managed now as a medical event to be delayed and a subject to be avoided, where Revelation names the rider, gives him a limit, and sets him under the authority of the Lamb who opened the seal.

expand to see more

The modern arrangement is to keep death out of sight: it happens in institutions, it is spoken of in euphemism, and the aim of a great deal of effort is to postpone the conversation rather than prepare for the event. Revelation 6:8 does the opposite. It paints the horse the colour of a corpse, names the rider Death, tells the reader that Hell followed with him, and states plainly how much power was given to them. Nothing about the vision is comfortable and everything about it is bounded — the power is given, the portion is a fourth, and the seal was opened by the Lamb that was slain.

Isaiah 29:22 is the counterweight and belongs preached beside it. God promises that the face of his people shall not wax pale, and he grounds it not in their strength but in his own prior act: the LORD who redeemed Abraham. The saint is not promised he will never see the pale horse; he is promised that shame will not have the last word in his countenance, because the redemption that took hold of Abraham has taken hold of him. A man who knows both verses can look steadily at a thing this culture cannot bear to name.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chavar (H2357), to grow pale; bosh (H954), to be ashamed; padah (H6299), to redeem; Greek chloros (G5515), pale green.

expand to see more

Hebrew chavar (H2357) — to blanch, to wax pale; what Jacob's face shall not do.

Hebrew bosh (H954) — to be ashamed, confounded; the shame paleness displays.

Hebrew padah (H6299) — to ransom, to redeem; the LORD who redeemed Abraham.

Greek chloros (G5515) — pale green, the colour of a corpse; the horse of the fourth seal.

Greek thanatos (G2288) — death; the only rider of the four who is given a name.

Usage

"“Neither shall his face now wax pale” — grounded in a redemption already done."

"“Behold a pale horse... his name that sat on him was Death” — named and bounded."

"“Power was given unto them” — given, and therefore limited."
